newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl repeats invite to SPD to talk again on tax.
newsitem.headline: Kohl repeats invite to SPD to talk again on tax.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl repeated an invitation on Wednesday to Germany's fractious opposition Social Democrats (SPD) to return to the negotiating table to discuss sweeping reforms to the country's tax system.
"The coalition is ready to resume talks at any time," Kohl told the Koelner Stadt-Anzeiger in an interview due to be published in full on Thursday.

Kohl's remarks followed overtures by some SPD leaders indicating the opposition's resistance is softening to coalition plans to slash the top rate of income tax as part of plans to cut taxes by 30 billion marks ($17.4 billion) over the next two years.

SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine has bowed to pressure from dovish premiers in SPD-ruled federal states and dropped his resistance to a cut in the 53 percent peak tax rate, as long as the cut is paid for through offsetting measures.

Lafontaine, who had tried to enforce a party line blocking any "tax giveaways for the rich", changed his position on the top rate of tax after powerful SPD figures, including rival Gerhard Schroeder, said compromise was needed.

Newspapers on Wednesday carried reports that the two had clashed at a party meeting on Monday after Schroeder said he would only represent the interests of his home state of Lower Saxony -- a comment interpreted as a refusal to toe the party line on tax.
The popular Schroeder is widely tipped to challenge Lafontaine for the right to stand as the SPD's candidate to become chancellor at the general election in October 1998.
Still unclear is how far the SPD would be prepared to go towards Finance Minister Theo Waigel's plan to cut the top rate of income tax to 39 percent in 1999.
The Berliner Morgenpost newspaper said SPD regional leaders would be ready to see the top rate fall to 46 percent.

Kohl, facing the obstacle of an SPD-led Bundesrat upper house of parliament, told the newspaper he would press ahead with his programme to legislate tax cuts whether or not a deal can be reached with the opposition party.

"That doesn't change our legislative timetable at all," he said. He added that extra sessions of the government-controlled Bundestag lower house would be called during the summer recess to press ahead with the legislation.
Germany's broad tax debate has no direct impact on its fitness to qualify for European monetary union (EMU) since the bulk of the tax cuts would come only in 1999.
Despite high unemployment and new figures showing that tax revenues in the first quarter were down 4.3 percent on a year earlier, Waigel reaffirmed Germany would make the cut for EMU.

"The budget deficit this year will be 2.9 percent of gross domestic product," Waigel wrote in the Bayernkurier, his Christian Social Union (CSU) party's newspaper. The Maastricht treaty sets a deficit limit of three percent of GDP.
SPD chief whip Peter Struck said, however, the government must freeze spending and pass a supplementary budget to get a grip on the deficit.
"Waigel doesn't have a serious financial policy," Struck told Deutschlandradio Berlin. "Last year's budget is no longer worth the paper it is written on." ($ = 1.724 German Marks)
